posts.copy:
90.2%. That is the share of SMIC's second-quarter revenue that came from China. A year earlier it was 84.1%.

That is not a chip story. It is a customer story.

Read from a desk in London or New York, the headline was export controls. Cut a foundry off from Western tools and Western customers, and it shrinks.

The filing says otherwise. Revenue was $3,005.6 million in the quarter, up 36.1% on a year earlier. Utilisation was 93.7%.

America fell from 12.9% of revenue to 8.2%. The business grew anyway.

The customers who replaced that revenue are not named in a results table. The mix gives a hint: industrial and automotive went from 10.6% of wafer revenue to 16.5% in a year.

That is the part you cannot read from outside. Who the domestic chip designers filling those lines are, what they are building for carmakers and factories, and how quickly they move from a design to an order.

Those answers sit in meeting rooms in China, not in a filing.

When a market loses its foreign customers and keeps growing, the demand did not disappear. It moved somewhere you are not looking.

If you want to see this on the ground for yourself, work with us.

DM us, or write to us at hello@oj.ventures

Source: SMIC results announcement, 13 August 2026

#China #Semiconductors #DeepTech #APAC

posts.copy:
Britain is supposed to be a hard market for a car brand nobody has heard of. Two Chinese brands passed 100,000 sales there this summer.

Omoda arrived at the end of August 2024. Jaecoo followed at the start of 2025. The 100,000 mark came in less than two years, at a combined share of nearly 5.7% of new registrations.

Nobody in Britain was waiting for these names. So the hard part was never the car. It was the buyer, and the route to that buyer.

The buyer was a household, not a fleet desk. Of the more than 36,500 Omoda 5s sold, 71% went to private retail customers.

The route was built early: 144 dealerships across the country. Their UK chief executive said it plainly. Getting there "would require investing heavily in our people, our retailer network and the ownership experience."

That is the pattern in most Asia-to-West moves we see. A new name does not earn trust from an advert. It earns it from a showroom down the road and someone to call when something goes wrong.

The buyer, the route to them, and the story they hear first. Rebuilding those three is what our GTM advisory work is for.

We have never worked with Omoda, Jaecoo or Chery. This is commentary from the outside.

If you want your move into the West to look like this, work with us.

DM us, or write to us at hello@oj.ventures

Source: Motoring Research, 13 August 2026

posts.copy:
Give us 45 minutes with a startup stuck in a corporate pilot in Asia and we can usually tell whether it will ever become a contract.

We start with four things:

→ Sponsor
→ Budget line
→ Success metric
→ Next signature

Then we look at what is underneath them.

Is your sponsor the person who owns the budget, or the person who liked the demo?

Is the pilot paid for from a line that exists next year, or from an innovation fund that has to be argued for again?

Was the success metric written down before the pilot started, by someone on their side?

Have you met procurement yet, or only the innovation team?

From the inside this looks like patience. The corporate is slow, so the answer must be to wait. Sometimes it is. More often the pilot was set up with nobody on the other side who could say yes, and no amount of waiting fixes that.

APAC is not one market. It is 15+ ecosystems with different rules, cultures and buyer behaviour, and the route to a signature changes with each one.

That hour usually tells us whether we are useful to you. Sometimes the answer is no.

If you are six months into a corporate pilot in APAC with no contract in sight, work with us.

DM us, or write to us at hello@oj.ventures

#APAC #Startups #Corporates #Founders
